title: Regional businesses strangled as operating costs skyrocket and profits plummet
full_text:
Australia’s regional businesses are being strangled by skyrocketing operating costs, declining profits and a web of regulatory red tape, the small business lobby says, pushing government to rethink its next round of tax hikes and provide further fuel excise relief.
The stark warning from the Council of Small Business Organisations comes as one of Australia’s largest banks said business conditions would remain rocky over the next year as interest rate hikes weighed down growth and war in Iran continued to put upward pressure on inflation. An annual report released by COSBOA on Friday found almost nine in 10 regional small businesses were weathering increased expenses, more than 70 per cent reported falling profit s and just 7 per cent believed cost pressures would ease in the next year.
Just under 40 per cent of businesses surveyed pointed to elevated fuel prices as a cause for concern, with war in the Middle East threatening to widen after Houthi strikes on commercial ships in the Red Sea.
With the government’s fuel excise relief scheduled to roll off at the end of the month, and the critical oil shipping route remaining shuttered, COSBOA chief executive Skye Cappuccio said any extension to the measure would be welcomed.
“I think small businesses, including small businesses in the regions, definitely have concerns about the ongoing impact of war in the Middle East and about fuel excise changes and what will happen when those changes revert to normal settings,” Ms Cappuccio told the Australian.
“We would welcome an extension of the current settings.” Westpac’s quarterly business signal released on Thursday similarly identified war in Iran as a key influence on Australia’s economic outlook, saying it would take time to restore Gulf oil production and shipping flows through the Strait.
The bank’s base case sees Brent Crude hovering around $US85 a barrel by the end of the year before easing to $US68 a barrel; under its adverse scenario where there is no resolution to the conflict, buffers in global oil markets fade and oil prices jump above their peak to $US148 a barrel by the end of 2026.
Westpac said conditions for small to medium enterprises were substantially weaker than those experienced by commercial and large corporates, as margins were squeezed by a “widening gap between revenue and expense growth”.
Jim Chalmers on Thursday conceded the economy was facing intensifying global pressures as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, as well as a set of “very substantial generational challenges”.
“The AI revolution, the energy transformation, the changes to our industrial base, the ageing of our population, the fragmenting of geopolitics, all of this presents parties of the sensible centre and the centre-left like the Australian Labor Party with a series of very serious economic challenges,” the Treasurer said.
COSBOA in its report pointed to workforce shortages as a key constraint for regional business growth, revealing almost 90 per cent of rural small businesses had experienced hiring challenges.
The labour market has remained fairly resilient in the face of slowing growth, resurgent inflation and three interest rate hikes, with jobs data released on Thursday showing unemployment steady at 4.4 per cent in June.
Among concerns raised by small businesses, operators pointed to growing compliance requirements and complex regulatory red tape as key inhibitors of growth and productivity. Labor now has its eyes set on a $45bn tax hike on trusts, which Ms Cappuccio said would be disastrous for small business. “We have very significant concerns about the impact of the minimum 30 per cent tax rate on discretionary trusts,” she said. “We have heard from multiples of those businesses about what the impact will be. Obviously for some that will affect whether it remains viable to continue. For others, it means they won’t be able to go ahead with things like planned investment. If we want stronger regional economies, we need policies that make it easier – not harder – for small businesses to invest, employ people and grow.”
